Before interpreting a fitted GLLVM, separate two questions. Did the
optimizer find a numerically healthy point estimate? Does the fitted
response distribution show an obvious mismatch to the three behavioural
responses arranged in long format? This article answers those questions for a small count example
before moving on to covariance, ordination, repeatability, or interval
claims.

Use these diagnostics to decide what to inspect or refit next, not as a
certificate that every inferential target is calibrated.

The example is deliberately modest: three behaviours counted on each
individual, fitted with one shared latent variable. `latent()` estimates a
low-rank axis of between-individual covariance; this is a diagnostic
example, not the full ordinary `latent()` covariance-decomposition
tutorial from [Morphometrics](morphometrics.html).

The counts fitted below are Poisson, so nothing here screens the response
before fitting. For binary or binomial traits, some conditions are worth
checking before you fit at all -- rare or constant outcomes, near-duplicate
or complementary columns, unusable denominators. `screen_gllvmTMB()` runs
that check; see the
[pre-fit response screening](pre-fit-response-screening.html) article for
the full walkthrough. Its threshold checks (prevalence, minority counts,
duplicate and complement pairs) are advisory: a flag is a hint to inspect
the design more closely, not a pass/fail verdict. The optional
fixed-design separation module (`screen_control(separation = "fixed")`)
is different in kind -- a formal certificate of overlap, complete, or
quasi-complete separation over coefficient-connected fixed-design blocks.
It does not inspect latent loadings or covariance and does not guarantee
convergence; coverage is fixed-design binomial blocks only, and overall
screening is partial.

## Setup

```{r setup}
library(gllvmTMB)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Fit A Small Model

The data have one row per `(individual, trait)` observation. The
working question is whether the three behaviours show a shared
between-individual axis and whether the fitted Poisson response model
looks reasonable enough to inspect.

```{r simulate}
set.seed(20260609)

n_ind <- 48L
trait_names <- c("forage", "alarm", "explore")
n_traits <- length(trait_names)

z <- rnorm(n_ind, sd = 0.45)
eta <- cbind(
  forage = 0.25 + 0.75 * z,
  alarm = -0.15 - 0.45 * z,
  explore = 0.05 + 0.55 * z
)
y <- matrix(
  rpois(n_ind * n_traits, lambda = exp(as.vector(eta))),
  nrow = n_ind,
  ncol = n_traits
)

df_long <- data.frame(
  individual = factor(rep(seq_len(n_ind), each = n_traits)),
  trait = factor(rep(trait_names, n_ind), levels = trait_names),
  count = as.vector(t(y))
)

head(df_long, 8)
```

The long-format call is canonical. It names the response, the trait
column, and the unit column explicitly.

```{r fit-long}
fit_long <- gllvmTMB(
  count ~ 0 + trait +
    latent(0 + trait | individual, d = 1),
  data = df_long,
  trait = "trait",
  unit = "individual",
  family = poisson(),
  control = gllvmTMBcontrol(n_init = 2, init_jitter = 0.03)
)

fit <- fit_long
fit
```

The same model can be fitted from a wide data frame with the
`traits(...)` left-hand side. The wide call is useful when the data
start as one row per individual and one column per behaviour.

```{r fit-wide}
df_wide <- stats::reshape(
  df_long,
  idvar = "individual",
  timevar = "trait",
  direction = "wide"
)
names(df_wide) <- sub("^count\\.", "", names(df_wide))

fit_wide <- gllvmTMB(
  traits(forage, alarm, explore) ~ 1 +
    latent(1 | individual, d = 1),
  data = df_wide,
  unit = "individual",
  family = poisson(),
  control = gllvmTMBcontrol(n_init = 2, init_jitter = 0.03)
)

signif(
  abs(as.numeric(logLik(fit_long)) - as.numeric(logLik(fit_wide))),
  3
)
```

The observed difference is about `2.14e-09`, which is negligible at the
reported precision: the two calls reach the same stacked-trait likelihood.

## Read Fit Health

The conservative convergence verdict is `fit$fit_health$converged`. It requires
an optimiser success code, a finite objective, and an unscaled maximum gradient
below `0.01`. `scaled_gradient` is retained as a descriptive diagnostic, but
objective scaling cannot turn a failed optimiser or a large raw gradient into a
usable optimum. Hessian curvature and `sdreport()` remain separate inference
checks.

```{r convergence-verdict}
data.frame(
  converged = isTRUE(fit$fit_health$converged),
  optimizer_converged = isTRUE(fit$fit_health$optimizer_converged),
  stationary_by_gradient = isTRUE(fit$fit_health$stationary_by_gradient),
  raw_max_gradient = signif(fit$fit_health$max_gradient, 4),
  raw_gradient_threshold = 0.01,
  scaled_gradient_descriptive = signif(fit$fit_health$scaled_gradient, 4)
)
```

`check_gllvmTMB()` returns the detailed, machine-readable fit-health table used
in simulations, tests, and reports. `gllvmTMB_diagnose()` instead prints a
guided narrative for an interactive first look. Start with either one before
interpreting coefficients, latent variables, or covariance summaries.

```{r fit-health}
health <- check_gllvmTMB(fit)
key_components <- c(
  "optimizer_convergence",
  "max_gradient",
  "sdreport",
  "pd_hessian",
  "weak_axis_unit",
  "boundary_sigma_eps"
)
health[
  health$component %in% key_components,
  c("component", "status", "message")
]
```

These six displayed rows are the headline fit-health checks for this example;
read each `status` column literally (`pd_hessian` warns here). The full table
contains more checks, so always inspect every warning rather than treating a
selected subset as the whole verdict. Here are all non-passing rows, including
their thresholds, meaning, and suggested action.

```{r fit-health-warnings}
health[
  health$status != "PASS",
  c("component", "status", "value", "threshold", "message", "action")
]
```

In this fit, the two warnings describe the same feature: the fitted
trait-specific diagonal standard deviation is almost zero. The simulation
planted a shared latent component without an additional trait-specific
between-individual component, so a boundary estimate is plausible here. It
still matters for interpretation: this example supports a shared axis, but it
does not demonstrate recovery of a separate diagonal variance. “Mapped off”
means a parameter was deliberately fixed or excluded from the fitted model,
rather than estimated near zero.

Read the rows literally. Optimizer and gradient rows speak to the
point estimate. `sdreport` and `pd_hessian` speak to Hessian-based
standard errors and Wald-style inference. A weak-axis row says a
latent variable explains only a small share of the fitted common covariance
and may therefore be hard to interpret; it does not by itself prove
that the fitted response distribution is wrong.

`optimizer_convergence` and `pd_hessian` are worth reading narrowly.
The `optimizer_convergence` row reports only the optimizer's exit code:
it says the optimizer stopped appropriately, not that the point
estimate is close to the true generating parameters. (The separate
`fit$fit_health$converged` list field is stricter -- it also requires a
finite objective and a small maximum gradient -- but the same reading
applies.) `pd_hessian` is a local curvature test at that point
estimate, not a global check. Read together, a clean table supports
"the optimizer stopped appropriately with locally consistent
curvature," not "this fit is near the truth."

For `ordinal_probit()` traits, the loading/variance degeneracy screen
shown above is binomial-only and does not run on ordinal rows, so a
degenerate ordinal fit can pass this table with no warning at all.
There is no calibrated ordinal degeneracy detector; see
[Current limits](current-limits.html) before treating an ordinal fit
as healthy.

`boundary_sigma_eps` checks the continuous-family residual scale when
that parameter is active. A warning means the estimate is below the
reported threshold, so the residual scale is close to its boundary; it
does not apply when the model or response family maps that parameter
off.

The same table records intentionally skipped standard errors. A no-SE
fit can still be useful for point estimates or refit-based uncertainty, such
as a bootstrap that repeatedly fits the model to new samples, but it should not
be reported as if Wald standard errors were computed.

```{r no-se-health}
fit_no_se <- gllvmTMB(
  count ~ 0 + trait +
    latent(0 + trait | individual, d = 1),
  data = df_long,
  trait = "trait",
  unit = "individual",
  family = poisson(),
  control = gllvmTMBcontrol(se = FALSE)
)

no_se_health <- check_gllvmTMB(fit_no_se)
no_se_health[
  no_se_health$component %in% c("sdreport", "pd_hessian", "max_fixed_se"),
  c("component", "status", "message")
]
```

For hard fits, move from this table to the
[Convergence and start values](convergence-start-values.html) article
before making scientific claims.

## When to try `loading_ridge = 2` {#loading-ridge-sensitivity}

Ordinary native Laplace fits stay unpenalised by default, equivalent to
`loading_ridge = Inf`. The control constructor keeps `loading_ridge = NULL`
to preserve that behaviour; it does not impose an infinitely strong penalty.
This section concerns ordinary Laplace fits. Opt-in AGHQ has its own
`aghq_ridge` default, described in `?gllvmTMBcontrol`.

Try `loading_ridge = 2` as a separate sensitivity fit when ordinary
between-unit latent loadings become extreme or change substantially between
fits. If a Hessian warning remains after checking the data, latent rank and
starting values, it is also reasonable to compare this fit, provided a loading
prior makes scientific sense. A better Hessian alone is not a reason to
choose the result: the prior can supply curvature that the data lack.

The setting puts a zero-mean normal prior with standard deviation 2,
variance 4, on free ordinary between-unit loadings. It favours smaller
loadings. Smaller positive settings shrink more, while `Inf` removes the
penalty. It does not penalise the trait-specific diagonal covariance or
silently extend to spatial, phylogenetic or within-unit loadings. It does not
repair separated fixed effects; see [When a rare species breaks the
JSDM](rare-species-jsdm.html).

### What the comparison found

A native-Laplace study fitted 6,000 datasets at each of `Inf`, `1`, `2` and
`4`: 24,000 attempts in total. It used six traits, two latent axes, estimated
trait-specific diagonal covariance and one latent predictor. There were
500 independent datasets per condition: grouped-binomial probit, replicated
Gaussian and replicated Poisson, with 100 or 400 units and two loading scales.
Failed fits and unavailable intervals stayed in the results.

| Loading prior SD | Attempts | Fits with unavailable trait-effect intervals |
|---|---:|---:|
| `Inf` | 6,000 | 64 |
| `1` | 6,000 | 56 |
| `2` | 6,000 | 66 |
| `4` | 6,000 | 62 |

All optimiser exit codes were zero. The unavailable intervals came from
non-positive-definite Hessians, illustrating why that code is insufficient
for inference. Ridge `2` restored intervals on 16 datasets relative to `Inf`
but lost them on 18 others. It did not improve availability overall.

Ridge `2` gave modest recovery gains. The largest observed reduction in mean
total-covariance error was in the strong-loading binomial condition with 100
units: relative matrix error fell from 0.255 to 0.237. Its paired reduction
was 0.0181, with Monte Carlo standard error 0.0021. Trait-effect estimates
changed little in the Gaussian conditions.

Coverage means the fraction of repeated datasets whose interval contains
the true effect. In the same small-sample binomial condition, the
nominal 95% interval for a zero effect covered it in 94.8% of available
intervals with `Inf`, 92.5% with `1`, 94.1% with `2` and 94.4% with `4`.
For a positive effect, coverage was 92.1%, 90.1%, 91.6% and 92.1%, respectively.
The coverage estimates have about one percentage point of Monte Carlo
uncertainty each. The `2` minus `Inf` differences in the fractions of all
attempts producing an interval containing truth were -0.6 percentage points
for the zero effect and -0.4 for the positive effect, with paired Monte Carlo
standard errors of about one percentage point. Thus the small differences
do not establish a clear coverage improvement or deterioration.

Stronger shrinkage can improve point recovery while narrowing intervals and
reducing coverage. The negative effect in the weak-loading Poisson condition
with 100 units retained about 91% coverage at every setting. The study does
not establish general 95% coverage, and its predictor-informed rank-two
results do not certify intercept-only ordination or latent-score intervals.
[Download the aggregated study tables and fixed-truth data generator](../loading-ridge-study-2026-10-18.zip)
for the condition-specific results, uncertainty summaries and provenance.
The archive contains aggregate tables, not raw fits or the complete fitting
materials.

### Compare the same model in either data shape

The following calls use the same data and rank as the earlier example.
They illustrate the sensitivity workflow; they do not repeat the coverage
study. Keep the original fit alongside the penalised fit.

```{r ridge-long-wide}
ridge_control <- gllvmTMBcontrol(
  n_init = 2, init_jitter = 0.03, loading_ridge = 2
)

# Long data: one row per individual and trait.
set.seed(20261018)
fit_ridge_long <- gllvmTMB(
  count ~ 0 + trait + latent(0 + trait | individual, d = 1),
  data = df_long, trait = "trait", unit = "individual",
  family = poisson(), control = ridge_control
)

# Wide data: the same model through traits().
set.seed(20261018)
fit_ridge_wide <- gllvmTMB(
  traits(forage, alarm, explore) ~ 1 + latent(1 | individual, d = 1),
  data = df_wide, unit = "individual",
  family = poisson(), control = ridge_control
)

# Compare trait-scale covariance, which does not depend on axis rotation.
covariance_sensitivity <- lapply(
  list(unpenalised = fit_long, ridge2 = fit_ridge_long),
  extract_Sigma, level = "unit", part = "total", link_residual = "none"
)
lapply(covariance_sensitivity, function(x) round(x$Sigma, 3))

# The long and wide ridge fits target the same covariance.
wide_covariance <- extract_Sigma(
  fit_ridge_wide, level = "unit", part = "total", link_residual = "none"
)
signif(max(abs(wide_covariance$Sigma -
               covariance_sensitivity$ridge2$Sigma)), 3)
check_gllvmTMB(fit_ridge_long)
```

Inspect whether covariance, fitted means and the effects you intend to report
change materially. For a model with `lv = ~ x`, compare
`extract_lv_effects(fit, type = "trait_effect")`; raw axis coefficients can
rotate between fits. If the result is sensitive, report that sensitivity and
consider the model structure and prior scale. Comparing `1`, `2`, `4` and
`Inf` can help; selecting a scale solely because its Hessian passes cannot
establish identification or interval calibration.

Finite ridge gives a maximum a posteriori estimate, rather than an ordinary
maximum-likelihood estimate. With matching retained curvature metadata,
trait-effect intervals are local approximate posterior intervals conditional
on the selected prior scale. Unsupported uncertainty remains unavailable.
Ordinary AIC, BIC and likelihood-ratio interpretations do not apply to these
penalised estimates. The default remains unpenalised.

## Check Response Diagnostics

Numerical convergence is not enough. For Gaussian, Poisson, and NB2 rows,
`residuals(type = "randomized_quantile")` evaluates each fitted family's
cumulative distribution function at the observed response. These are exact
CDF calculations at the fitted parameter values and fitted random-effect modes,
but they do not propagate parameter, refit, or random-effect uncertainty and
are not a formal calibration test. NB1 uses the same implemented exact-CDF
route and has a display smoke test, but it has not yet reached the same depth of
evidence as Gaussian, Poisson, and NB2. `diagnostic_table()` turns the attached
metadata into ordinary data frames for reports and articles.

| Family | `type = "randomized_quantile"` result | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Gaussian | Exact family-CDF residual | Established |
| Poisson | Exact family-CDF residual | Established |
| NB2 | Exact family-CDF residual | Established |
| NB1 | Exact family-CDF residual, same route | Implemented, shallower evidence |
| Every other family | No exact residual: the row is retained with `status = "unsupported_family"` and `residual = NA`; request `type = "simulation_rank"` explicitly for a simulation-based check | Simulation-based route available, not exact |
| Missing response / non-finite observed value | No residual computed | Row retained with an explicit `status`, never silently dropped |

```{r residual-table}
rq <- residuals(
  fit,
  type = "randomized_quantile",
  seed = 20260609
)

diagnostic_table(rq, table = "row_status")
diagnostic_table(rq, table = "fit_health_status")

head(
  diagnostic_table(rq, table = "data")[
    , c("trait", "family", "observed", "residual", "status")
  ],
  8
)
```

The `row_status` table tells you whether every model row produced a
usable residual. If a row is marked `unsupported_family`,
`missing_response`, or `nonfinite_observed`, keep that status in the
report rather than silently dropping the row.

The Q-Q points below stay broadly near the reference line through the centre,
but the alarm and forage panels depart in the upper tail. The display is useful
because it does not turn a mostly straight pattern into a blanket pass: those
tails deserve inspection, and the plot is not evidence that the latent rank or
uncertainty estimates are calibrated.

```{r residual-qq, fig.class="wide-scientific-figure", fig.cap = "Randomized-quantile residual Q-Q check for the fitted Poisson GLLVM. This is a fitted-model diagnostic display, not interval calibration, latent-rank proof, or a Bayesian posterior predictive check."}
predictive_check(
  fit,
  type = "rq_qq",
  seed = 20260609
)
```

For Poisson and NB2 count models, a rootogram is often easier to read than a
Q-Q plot. Bars near zero mean the observed and fitted-model simulated count
frequencies are similar on the square-root scale. The simulations default to
`condition_on_RE = TRUE`, so they condition on the fitted random-effect modes;
they check the fitted response pattern, not the marginal random-effect
distribution. The plot below shows noticeable alternating discrepancies,
especially for forage counts 3 and 5. They do not all point in one direction,
but they are large enough to investigate rather than dismiss. Simulation noise
remains, even with the larger draw count used here.

```{r rootogram, fig.class="wide-scientific-figure", fig.cap = "Rootogram comparing observed behavioural counts with simulations conditional on the fitted random-effect modes. Persistent departures can flag a response-family, link, covariate, offset, or fitted-linear-predictor mismatch; this display does not test the marginal random-effect distribution."}
predictive_check(
  fit,
  type = "rootogram",
  ndraws = 200,
  seed = 20260609,
  max_count = 7L
)
```

### Coming From DHARMa

If DHARMa is your reference point from glmmTMB workflows, the rough
correspondence is: DHARMa's simulation-based residuals map to
`residuals(fit, type = "simulation_rank")`, and DHARMa's diagnostic plots
map to `predictive_check(fit, ...)`. This is a conceptual mapping, not
DHARMa compatibility -- gllvmTMB does not wrap or reproduce DHARMa, and it
does not currently provide DHARMa's formal uniformity, dispersion, or
outlier tests. Never treat the two as equivalent. Predictive plots here
are diagnostic display only: no interval calibration, latent-rank proof,
or DHARMa-equivalent formal test.

## What To Do Next

Use the diagnostics as routing information, not as a single pass/fail
stamp.

| What you see | What it means | Next step |
|---|---|---|
| The four numerical rows shown above all pass | The numerical fit is a reasonable starting point, provided the remaining rows contain no unexplained warnings | Inspect every non-PASS row, then inspect `Sigma`, correlations, ordination, or fitted effects. |
| Optimizer or gradient rows warn/fail | The point estimate may be unstable | Try more starts, rescaling, simpler rank, or an alternative optimizer. |
| `sdreport` or `pd_hessian` warns | Wald uncertainty is unavailable or local curvature may be unreliable | Inspect the scientific target and use a supported profile or refit-based bootstrap route where available. |
| Residual rows have non-`ok` status | Some rows were not diagnosed | Inspect missing values, non-finite responses, and family support. |
| Q-Q or rootogram shows systematic structure | The fitted conditional response pattern may be wrong | Revisit family, link, covariates, offsets, or the fitted linear predictor; investigate random effects separately. |

If the fit-health and response checks are acceptable but the latent rank
is still a modelling choice, continue to
[How many latent dimensions should I fit?](model-selection-latent-rank.html).
That article compares one ML candidate set with AIC/BIC and uses REML
only after a Gaussian model has been chosen.

## What A Simulation Check Can Establish

Simulation is useful only when its question is named. Three common checks
answer different questions:

| Check | What it can show | What it cannot show |
|---|---|---|
| Fitted-model predictive draw | Selected response patterns | Biological truth, latent rank, or interval calibration |
| Fitted-model simulate--refit | Local pipeline self-consistency | Real-data truth or protection against misspecification |
| Predeclared known-DGP grid | Bias, recovery, and interval performance in the studied regime | Performance outside the regimes actually studied |

One simulated dataset is an illustration, not recovery evidence. A validation
study needs repeated independent datasets, an estimand that matches the fitted
model, and separate counts for attempted fits, healthy fits, usable intervals,
and successful coverage. It should also report Monte Carlo uncertainty rather
than turning a small number of replicates into a pass/fail certificate.

This page covers fit health and no-SE status, fitted-model predictive
diagnostics and residuals for Gaussian, Poisson, and NB2 rows, and report-ready
metadata tables. NB1 uses an implemented exact-CDF route, but its evidence is
currently shallower than for those three families.

The page does not calibrate confidence intervals, prove the latent rank, run
formal residual tests, test the marginal random-effect distribution, or draw
from a Bayesian posterior. Exact residual support for delta, hurdle, truncated,
ordinal, and mixture-family rows remains outside its current claims.
